races.long_description: Representative Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, is trying to hold on to his seat in Alabama, which was redrawn after the Supreme Court decision that weakened provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to favor Republicans like his opponent, Rhett Marques. Republicans hope that this new district, with more white, conservative, rural voters, will be easier to flip.

Representative Nick Begich, a Republican in his first term, faces a challenge from Bill Hill, a fisherman and former school administrator who is mounting a competitive campaign as an independent candidate. They will appear alongside two other candidates on Alaska’s top-four ranked-choice ballot.

Jay Feely, a Republican and former N.F.L. kicker, is trying to defend a Republican-held district in Arizona that includes Scottsdale and a chunk of Phoenix. He faces Dr. Amish Shah, a moderate Democrat and former sideline doctor for the New York Jets.

Representative Juan Ciscomani, a two-term G.O.P. incumbent, is fighting to hold this southeastern district anchored in the suburbs of Tucson. Mr. Ciscomani is facing a challenge from JoAnna Mendoza, who has emphasized her background as a former Marine and her experience growing up in poverty.

Representative Kevin Kiley, a former Republican who this year became an independent, is facing Richard Pan, a former Democratic state senator, in California’s newly redrawn Sixth Congressional District. The district is widely considered favorable to Democrats and includes the city of Sacramento.

Two Democrats are going head to head in this Sacramento district after no Republicans advanced in an open primary. Representative Doris Matsui, 82, faces a generational challenge from Mai Vang, a City Council member who is more than 40 years her junior.

Connie Chan, a San Francisco supervisor, received a pivotal endorsement in the race to succeed Representative Nancy Pelosi, whose seat is open for the first time since 1987: Ms. Pelosi herself. Ms. Chan and her opponent, State Senator Scott Wiener, are liberal Democrats who share a desire to expand rights for immigrants and gay and transgender people but differ on housing and public transit policy.

Representative Adam Gray, a moderate Democrat who won the seat by fewer than 200 votes two years ago, is facing Kevin Lincoln, a Republican former mayor of Stockton, Calif., who after running unsuccessfully in 2024 is trying again, in a different district.

Representative David Valadao, a Republican, has survived several efforts to oust him from his seat in California’s Central Valley. Democrats hope that Randy Villegas, a progressive political scientist and school board trustee, can succeed on a map that was redrawn to make Mr. Valadao more vulnerable.

The redrawing of California’s congressional map strengthened the position of Representative George Whitesides, a Democrat in northern Los Angeles County. Kamala Harris carried the district by four percentage points in 2024, but would have won by 10 using the new map. Mr. Whitesides faces Jason Gibbs, a Republican city councilman from Santa Clarita.

Two Republican incumbents, Representatives Young Kim and Ken Calvert, face off in a bid for their political survival after being drawn into the same district by California’s redistricting plan, which favored Democrats. The district, which includes parts of Riverside and Orange counties, is one of the few remaining favorable districts for Republicans in California.

This district is currently held by a Republican, but the new version, redrawn last year to shift its boundaries from Riverside County west into Los Angeles County, leans heavily Democratic. Representative Linda Sánchez, a Democrat who represents half of the new district, is running for re-election against the Republican Mitch Clemmons, a plumber.

Representative Derek Tran, an Army veteran and Democrat, is well-positioned to win re-election in his Orange County district, which was redrawn last year. He has also far outraised his Republican opponent, the former mayor of Cerritos, Chuong Vo.

The seat of Representative Dave Min, an Orange County Democrat, is more solidly Democratic than it was in the last election cycle, before it was redrawn. He faces Jenny Rae Le Roux, a Republican businesswoman.

Representative Jeff Hurd, who lost President Trump’s endorsement after opposing his tariffs but regained it after a lobbying campaign by party leaders, is running for re-election. Recent polling suggests he’s in a tight race against his Democratic challenger, Dwayne Romero, an Army veteran and a former Aspen city councilman.

Representative Lauren Boebert, an ally of President Trump’s who in 2024 hopscotched into this district from another, handily won her previous election and is favored to win again. She faces Eileen Laubacher, a Democratic Navy veteran, and Douglas Mangeris, a libertarian construction superintendent.

Representative Jeff Crank, a freshman Republican, is running for re-election in a district that has shifted left in recent years amid population growth in Colorado Springs. Strong fund-raising by his Democratic challenger, Jessica Killin, an Army veteran, has further narrowed the race, which both parties now view as competitive.

Republican Representative Gabe Evans is trying for a second term against progressive Democrat Manny Rutinel, in a House district north of Denver that mixes working-class communities with ranches and farms. Mr. Evans is a top target of House Democrats, and a win by him would be a significant setback for the party.

Representative Kathy Castor, a 10-term Democrat who has never faced a close race, is running for re-election in a district in the Tampa area that was redrawn to favor Republicans. She faces Mike Beltran, a Republican former state representative, in a district that Mr. Trump won by about 11 points.

Representative Byron Donalds is giving up his red seat in Southwest Florida to run for governor. The favorite to fill it is Jim Schwartzel, a radio station owner who prevailed in the Republican primary over a Trump-backed candidate and two scandal-plagued former congressmen. He faces Victor Arias, a Democratic lawyer.

Casey Askar, a Republican businessman and former Marine, and Pia Dandiya, a Democrat and former high school principal, are vying to represent a district redrawn by Republican state lawmakers. The new district stretches west from Broward County across the Florida peninsula to Marco Island, on the state’s Gulf Coast.

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a two-term Democrat, is fighting to keep his seat after state Republicans redrew the congressional map to favor themselves. Scott Singer, a Republican former mayor, and Peter Jassenoff, the Libertarian candidate, are hoping to win in a district where voters favored Trump in 2024 but rejected him in 2020.

Representative María Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican, faces a challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, a first-time candidate and Democrat, in a Miami-based district that leans Republican but has been rocked by the Trump administration’s mass deportations.

Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican who won re-election by just 799 votes in 2024, faces Christina Bohannan, a Democrat, for a third consecutive election. Major Republican super PACs withdrew millions in planned spending from the southeastern Iowa district, signaling growing doubts about the incumbent’s prospects.

Representative Zach Nunn, a two-term Republican and a Trump ally, faces Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and a Lutheran minister, in a closely watched Des Moines-area district. Democrats see an opportunity to flip the seat amid growing economic discontent and frustration with the war in Iran.

Democrats invested heavily in the campaign of Zach Dembo, viewing his background as a Navy veteran, a former federal prosecutor and a former official under Gov. Andy Beshear as helpful for winning over swing voters. He is running in this conservative district against Dr. Ralph Alvarado, a Trump-backed physician and a former state senator.

The retirement of a conservative Democrat in this large, rural congressional district has given Republicans one of their best pickup opportunities of the cycle. Former Gov. Paul LePage, a Tea Party stalwart who is seen as a prime G.O.P recruit, is facing Matt Dunlap, the progressive state auditor.

Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican retired Army officer, is fighting to hold on to his seat in a swing district that Democrats have targeted for a pickup. He faces Will Lawrence, a progressive activist who beat out two more moderate Democrats for the party’s nomination.

Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet, a Democrat, is running for a second term in a district that voted for President Trump in 2024. Her Republican opponent, Tom Smith, won his nomination in unusual fashion: He had initially suspended his campaign, but still managed to beat Trump’s favored candidate, Amir Hassan.

Representative John James, a Republican, is running for governor, leaving open his highly competitive seat in suburban Detroit. Democrats have nominated Christina Hines, a prosecutor, to take on Michael Bouchard, a Republican Army veteran.

Sam Forstag, a Democrat backed by progressives like Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is bidding to replace the retiring Republican incumbent and flip a seat long held by conservatives. Mr. Forstag’s candidacy against Aaron Flint, a Trump-endorsed Republican, is a test for a theory that left-leaning politicians running in G.O.P. strongholds can do better in general elections than moderates.

The G.O.P. has all but ceded the seat held by Representative Don Bacon, a moderate Republican who is retiring, by withdrawing cash from his district. Denise Powell, a Democratic political organizer, is favored to defeat Brinker Harding, a Republican Omaha city councilman.

Representative Mark Amodei is retiring, and a Democrat has never represented his conservative northern Nevada district. But David Flippo, an Air Force veteran who emerged from the Republican primary with President Trump’s backing, has been weighed down by scandal, giving Teresa Benitez-Thompson, a Democratic former state legislator, hopes of pulling off an upset.

races.seat_description: North Las Vegas and central counties

races.long_description: Representative Jeff Van Drew joined the Republican Party after voting against President Trump’s impeachment in 2019. He won by 17 points in 2024. Zack Mullock, the mayor of Cape May, N.J., is hoping to flip the seat as a Democrat — just as Mr. Van Drew did in the 2018 midterms.

races.seat_description: Northern border; most of Bergen County

races.long_description: Representative Thomas Kean Jr., a Republican, is defending his seat against a strong challenge from Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy pilot who won the Democratic nomination in a romp. Mr. Kean’s campaign lost ground this spring when he was hospitalized for depression, leading him to miss months on Capitol Hill.

races.seat_description: Santa Fe with north and east counties

races.long_description: Representative Nick LaLota, a Republican, is running for a third term in a reliably red district extending to the eastern tip of Long Island. The race drew national attention in September when his opponent, Chris Gallant, admitted to posing in an explicit ad campaign modeling bondage gear almost two decades ago.

races.seat_description: Parts of Nassau County and Queens
races.long_description: Two years after Representative Tom Suozzi, a Democrat, narrowly defeated the Republican Mike LiPetri in New York’s Third Congressional District, which includes a section of Long Island and a sliver of Queens, the two are facing a rematch. Mr. Suozzi first won the seat in 2016, vacated it in 2022 to run for governor and reclaimed it in 2024.

After narrowly flipping a Republican-held seat two years ago, Representative Laura Gillen is running to retain her post in New York’s Fourth Congressional District, which includes portions of Nassau County on Long Island. Ms. Gillen is being challenged by Jeanine Driscoll, a Republican and the receiver of taxes in the town of Hempstead.

races.seat_description: North Brooklyn and parts of Queens

races.long_description: Eight years after Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a democratic socialist, surged to prominence by defeating a party stalwart in Queens, she will face off against a little-known and underfunded Republican real estate developer, Diamant Hysenaj. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez appears unconcerned by the challenge and has spent much of this election season campaigning for other Democrats.

Representative Mike Lawler, a Republican, has defied political odds by holding on to a suburban New York district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. This year he is facing a challenge from Cait Conley, a Democrat and a military veteran who has sought to tie Mr. Lawler to President Trump.

Few expected the race to replace Representative Elise Stefanik, who is not seeking re-election, to be close. But her upstate district, which stretches from the suburbs of Albany to the Canadian border, has been hit hard by President Trump’s tariffs, giving Democrats hope that Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer, can beat Anthony Constantino, a Trump-backed Republican businessman.

Representative Don Davis, a centrist Democrat, faces a challenge from Laurie Buckhout, a Republican and a retired Army colonel who narrowly lost to him in 2024. The district has elected Black Democrats since 1992, but North Carolina Republicans have since redrawn it to favor their party.

Representative Chuck Edwards, a Republican, dropped his re-election bid after the House Ethics Committee released a damning report about his inappropriate conduct toward young female staff members. Republicans have struggled to unify around their replacement candidate, Jennifer Balkcom, a state lawmaker. Her Democratic opponent, Jamie Ager, a farmer, has been leading in recent polling.

Representative Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in Congress, is in a rematch against Derek Merrin, a former G.O.P. state lawmaker who challenged her two years ago and lost. This time, Mr. Merrin faces Ms. Kaptur in a newly drawn district that gives Republicans an edge.

Representative Brian Fitzpatrick has been a Republican survivor in a suburban Philadelphia district where President Trump is unpopular. Now Mr. Fitzpatrick faces one of his toughest tests in years against Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner who has tried to make the race about stopping Republican control of Congress.

Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a first-term Republican, is facing Bob Brooks, a Democratic firefighter and union leader, in a competitive Lehigh Valley district. Mr. Mackenzie narrowly flipped the district two years ago but now faces scrutiny from voters over soaring costs and the war with Iran.

Representative Rob Bresnahan, a first-term Republican representing one of the country’s most competitive districts, is being challenged by Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton. She has accused Mr. Bresnahan, who campaigned on banning stock-trading by members of Congress but became one of the most active traders on Capitol Hill, of profiting from his position.

Representative Scott Perry, considered one of the most vulnerable House Republicans, two years ago narrowly defeated Janelle Stelson, a former news anchor. Now Ms. Stelson, a Democrat who has run ads embracing parts of Trump’s agenda, is waging a second campaign against Mr. Perry.

races.seat_description: State College and rural north central

races.long_description: Nancy Lacore, a Democratic former Navy admiral who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is running against Jenny Costa Honeycutt, a Republican Trump ally. They are facing off in a historically conservative district that was recently gerrymandered to favor Republicans. Still, Democrats believe Ms. Lacore has a chance to flip the seat.

races.seat_description: Parts of Columbia and southwest counties
East Houston and rural East Texas
Texas Panhandle to Denton County suburbs

races.long_description: Bobby Pulido, an award-winning Tejano singer, is challenging Representative Monica De La Cruz, a third-term Republican. Running as a conservative Democrat, Mr. Pulido has emphasized that he supports gun rights and border security while embracing Democratic calls for social welfare programs. Polls indicate a competitive race in a district that President Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

A Republican firearms influencer, Brandon Herrera, is in a tight race with Katy Padilla Stout, a lawyer and former teacher who has highlighted Mr. Herrera’s absolutist views on gun regulations and his inflammatory online rhetoric. Mr. Herrera has cast her as too liberal for a West Texas border district that President Trump won by 15 points in 2024.

races.seat_description: Fort Worth suburbs and North Texas
Laredo and the Rio Grande Valley
races.long_description: Representative Henry Cuellar, an 11-term Democrat, is defending a South Texas district where voters favored President Trump by 10 percentage points in 2024. He is facing Tano Tijerina, the Webb County judge, who changed his party affiliation to Republican from Democrat after Mr. Trump was re-elected in 2024.

Representative Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat, is defending his seat in a South Texas district that was redrawn to be more favorable to Republicans. His opponent, Eric Flores, is a Trump-endorsed former federal prosecutor and Army veteran.

Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is trying to deliver an open seat anchored in San Antonio to Republicans, who redrew the district last year to lean red. His opponent, Johnny Garcia, is a former deputy sheriff running as a conservative Democrat.
Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor pitching herself as a law-and-order Democrat, is challenging Representative Rob Wittman, a 10-term Republican, in one of the nation’s most competitive House races.

Representative Jen Kiggans, a Republican, is in a rematch against Elaine Luria, the former Democratic representative she unseated four years ago. The two Navy veterans are vying to represent Virginia’s tidewater district, which is deeply intertwined with the U.S. military and affected by the Iran War.

Representative John McGuire, a first-term Republican, faces former Representative Tom Perriello, a Democrat who held a similar seat during the Obama administration, in a race that could signal Democrats’ strength this year. President Trump carried the district, which stretches from Charlottesville to the border with North Carolina, by 12 points in 2024.

Representative Eugene Vindman, a freshman Democrat, is vying to keep his seat. While Virginia’s top court struck down a new congressional map that would have rendered his district more safely blue, the national political environment this year is favorable for Democrats. Mr. Vindman faces Doug Ollivant, a Republican Army veteran.

Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate Democrat who has regularly broken with her party to work across the aisle, won her southwestern Washington seat twice against a hard-line Republican. Now, she’s fighting for a third term against John Braun, a Republican state legislative leader endorsed by President Trump.

Representative Bryan Steil, a Republican, is trying to fend off a challenge from Mitchell Berman, a Democrat who is a nurse. Republicans have held the southeastern Wisconsin district for three decades, but Democrats have gained ground there in recent years.

Representative Derrick Van Orden, a hard-line Republican who attended the Jan. 6, 2021, rally at the Capitol, is facing Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat whom he defeated in 2024. The rural western Wisconsin district went for President Trump the last three elections, but Democrats consider this a prime opportunity to flip it.

text.paragraph: First results from the state usually come in around 10 p.m. Eastern time. Most voters cast ballots by mail, and full, unofficial counting typically takes days.

Most voters tend to vote early in person, and vote reporting is usually relatively fast. But if a race is very close, it can still take awhile to declare a winner. In 2022, it took until Wednesday afternoon for The A.P. to declare that the top Senate candidates had advanced to a runoff, which was held on Dec. 6.
In 2022 and 2024, about half of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and the count reached 95 percent around 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

In 2024, just under half of voters cast ballots by mail, and it took about two days to report 95 percent of votes statewide. Postmarked ballots must arrive by the fourth day after the election, Nov. 7.
In 2024, 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported just after midnight on election night. Procedural changes could make that even faster this year.

In the past two general elections, 97 percent of the state’s votes were counted by noon Eastern time the day after the election. Counting has sped up since 2020, when it took several days to finish counting mail ballots.

In 2024, 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported by 5 a.m. Eastern time the morning after the election. In some places, absentee ballots are counted at a central facility and reported in large batches.
Most results are typically reported by 1 a.m. Eastern time, and congressional races in recent general elections have been called by The Associated Press on election night.

First results are expected around 1 a.m. Eastern time. In 2024, about 75 percent of votes were reported on election night, and the remaining votes were reported between seven and fifteen days later. Ranked-choice voting is used in federal and state races; if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, the next tabulation will be conducted on Nov. 18.
Most results are typically reported by early Wednesday morning, and recent congressional races have all been called by The A.P. on election night.

Most voters cast votes by mail, and ballots can take days — or even weeks — to count. Counties have until the 13th day after the election to report their votes, with some exceptions. During the state’s June primaries, this slow process fostered suspicion when two candidates flipped positions five days into vote counting — a phenomenon that is common with election results but usually happens quickly on election night.

The state has long conducted its elections by mail. In 2022 and in 2024, it took about four days to report 95 percent of votes in statewide races. If a race is close, it could take awhile for The A.P. to call a winner.

In 2024, it took a day and a half before 95 percent of votes were counted. But because the state’s congressional races were not especially competitive, they were all called by The A.P. on election night or in the early morning after.
Votes are reported fast, with nearly all ballots counted before midnight in recent elections.

In 2024, about 87 percent of votes were reported by noon Wednesday. The district recently implemented ranked-choice voting, so if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote in certain races, it could take days before additional tabulations are released.
Votes are counted very quickly, with 99 percent of votes reported by midnight in recent general elections. First votes are expected after most polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern time.
The state runs a predominantly mail election. In 2024, it took until about 4 p.m. Eastern time on Wednesday to reach 95 percent of votes. In 2022, it took an additional day.
First results from the state are expected after 11 p.m. Eastern time. In 2022 and 2024, most results were reported by Wednesday afternoon.
In 2024, nearly 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have two weeks to arrive.
First results from the state are expected after most polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time. In 2022 and 2024, most ballots were counted by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
In 2024, 90 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time, and 99 percent were in by noon Wednesday. One extremely close House race went to a recount and took weeks to decide.
Most votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday in 2022 and 2024. Mail ballots have three days to arrive if postmarked by Election Day, but only about one in 10 voters cast them.
First results from the state are expected after most polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time. In 2024, nearly all votes were counted by midnight on election night.

Most votes are typically reported by midnight Eastern time on election night. Elections for the state’s six U.S. House seats will be open primaries; if no candidate receives a majority of the vote, the top two vote-getters will advance to a Dec. 12 election.

In 2024, it took about a day and a half to reach 95 percent of votes. Ranked choice will be used in the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races, and only first rankings will be available; if no candidate receives a majority, a second tabulation will occur in the days after the election. In 2024, the results of a House race that required a second round were released 10 days after the election.
In 2024, 80 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, and it took several days to reach 95 percent of votes. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have 10 days to arrive.

In 2024, about two-thirds of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, but officials said a longer ballot this year could take more time to process. Ballots postmarked by Election Day have three days to arrive.

In 2024, 56 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and complete unofficial results were in by noon the next day. The deadline for hand-returning absentee ballots on Election Day is now 6 p.m. Eastern time instead of when the polls close.

In 2024, 84 percent of votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night. But because the state’s congressional races are not typically competitive, The A.P. tends to call them not long after polls close.
Most results are typically reported by early Wednesday morning, and recent congressional races have all been called by The A.P. on election night.
Most voters cast ballots by mail, which must be received by Election Day. In recent elections, it has taken a day or two to count 95 percent of the votes.
In 2024, about 60 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and 95 percent were in by 5 a.m.
Vote counting was faster in 2024 than in 2022, with three-quarters of the state’s votes reported by midnight on election night, and 93 percent reported by noon the next day.
In 2024, 91 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight on election night, and 96 percent were in by noon the next day.

By 1 a.m. Eastern time, processing of absentee ballots must either conclude, or pause and resume the next day. In the last two general elections, nearly all unofficial results were reported by noon Eastern time the day after the election.
Most votes are expected by noon on Wednesday. Mail ballots have a week to arrive if postmarked by Election Day, but only about one in 10 voters cast them in 2024.
In recent general elections, nearly all unofficial results were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.

In recent general elections, 95 percent of votes were reported by midnight Eastern time. Officials expect nearly all unofficial votes to be counted before they leave for the night, because absentee ballots are now due on Election Day instead of four days later (if postmarked). In 2024, it took more than two weeks for the A.P. to call a winner in an extremely close race.
In recent general elections, nearly all votes have been reported by midnight Eastern time on election night.
In recent elections, it has taken more than a week to reach 95 percent of votes counted. The state conducts all-mail elections, and ballots postmarked by Election Day have seven days to arrive.
Most votes are typically counted by around midnight Eastern time on election night.
Most votes are typically counted by midnight Eastern time on election night.
First results are expected after 9 p.m. Eastern time. More than one-third of voters cast ballots by mail in 2024, and 92 percent of votes were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
Most votes are typically counted by midnight Eastern time on election night.

In recent elections, 80 to 90 percent of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time, and 99 percent were in before 7 a.m. the day after the election. Voting by mail requires a valid excuse, and only a small share of voters cast ballots this way.

Most voters cast ballots by mail or dropbox, and it has typically taken more than a week to count 95 percent of votes. New rules requiring officials to verify the last four digits of voters' Social Security or driver's license numbers are expected to extend that timeline.
Nearly all votes are typically counted by noon Eastern time the day after the election.
In recent elections, the state reached 95 percent of votes reported on election night or in the early morning hours after.

In recent general elections, it has taken about eight days to report 95 percent of the state’s votes. Nearly all voters cast ballots by mail or drop box, and ballots with a postmark have 20 days to arrive.
In recent general elections, more than 95 percent of votes have been reported by midnight Eastern time.
In recent general elections, full unofficial results were reported by noon Eastern time on Wednesday.
Ranked-choice tabulation will occur on Nov. 18.

text.paragraph: Democrats’ prospects for taking control of the U.S. House have grown in recent months, with dozens of Republican-held districts in play.
Our election model estimates the outcome of the race in real time based on polling data, the votes reported so far and what we expect from remaining votes.
Democrats have won their target number of competitive districts and are on track to win the House.

paragraphs.paragraph: Republicans have an uphill battle to maintain control of the House — they would need to win most of the districts below, many of which were rated as leaning toward Democrats before the election.

contents.8: 27pmThe Needle is backOur live forecast is estimating the outcome of the presidential race, based on pre-election data, the votes reported so far, and the votes we think remain. Almost all of the vote counted so far points toward a very close election.9:17pmThe Needle’s early takeTrump is now a narrow but clear favorite to win Georgia and North Carolina. If he does, Harris would probably need to sweep the three Northern swing states — a real possibility, but a tall order.10:43pmHarris’s path narrowsTrump is very likely to take Georgia and North Carolina. To win, Harris will probably need to sweep Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin — but Trump has an advantage in all three.11:19pmHarris’s path narrowsTrump has won in North Carolina and is very likely to take Georgia. To win, Harris will probably need to sweep Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin — but Trump has an advantage in all three.12:50amThe U.S. shifts to the rightIn every state that has counted most of its votes, Trump has improved on his performance from 2020. content.text: Representative Jared Moskowitz, a centrist Democrat, will remain in Congress after defeating Scott Singer, a Republican, in a South Florida congressional district that had been redrawn by the state’s Republicans to favor their party, according to The Associated Press.

Moskowitz, one of the most prominent Jewish Democrats in Congress, chose to run in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, which stretches along the Atlantic coastline from Miami-Dade to Palm Beach Counties, after Republicans eliminated his former district.

There is no race where more is on the line for Elon Musk than the Senate election in Texas, where most polls just closed. Musk spent over $200 million to try to elect Ken Paxton to the Senate in his home state. Musk has laid out nearly $500 million during the midterms overall, the second-biggest expenditure by a donor even in a campaign cycle. The Texas result is a big test not just of Musk’s influence, but whether enormous political spending truly makes a difference.

Juliana Stratton, the Democratic lieutenant governor of Illinois, defeated Don Tracy, a former state Republican Party chairman, in the state’s Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Stratton’s victory means that next year, three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time — a first in the institution’s history.
When she takes office, she will serve alongside Senator Tammy Duckworth, a Thai American, making Illinois the first state represented by two women of color in the Senate at the same time.

Polls have closed in Texas, except for El Paso, which is one hour behind. Early vote results will come in first, but several counties will not release even those counts until every person in line has voted.

Kansas, where polls closed at 8 p.m. Eastern, has been reliably red in federal races, but the state has moved leftward in recent years and has had a Democratic governor since 2019. The Senate race between Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, and Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger, will hinge on counties Democrats have carried in presidential races, as well as areas that supported the re-election of Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, in 2022 and voted for President Trump two years later.
Johnson County

, a suburb of Kansas City where Hamilton lives, will account for over a quarter of the vote. Democrats won Johnson by over eight percentage points in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, but Hamilton is looking to make even more inroads there. In the 2022 governor’s race, Kelly won it by 20 points.
Sedgwick County
, which contains Wichita, is a key bellwether and a target for both candidates: Kelly won the county by three points, while Trump won it by more than 13 in 2024.
Shawnee County

, which contains Topeka, could provide an early read on the race; in 2024 it had mostly finished reporting its votes by 10 p.m. Eastern. Like Sedgwick, it was much bluer in the governor’s race: Kelly carried it by about 20 points, while Kamala Harris won it by less than one.

Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, easily won a second term as governor of Pennsylvania, defeating Stacy Garrity, the Republican state treasurer, The Associated Press reported. Given Shapiro’s broad favorability and huge fund-raising advantage, the outcome of the race was never in much doubt. This freed Shapiro to campaign for Democrats hoping to flip U.S. House seats in his crucial swing state, a gesture that could help his standing with Democrats nationwide should he decide to run for president in 2028.
A possible stunner may be brewing in the
South Carolina Senate race

, where Annie Andrews, the Democrat, has a narrow lead over Senator Darline Graham, the Republican, according to our estimates. While it’s still early, Andrews has done better than expected in the early vote, absentee vote and, crucially, in the first precincts to report on Election Day.

Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, a billionaire Democrat who is widely believed to be weighing a run for president, won a third term, The Associated Press reported. Pritzker prevailed in a rematch of his 2022 race with Darren Bailey, a Republican former state senator, in a solidly Democratic state. Pritzker has repeatedly sparred with President Trump, including when the president sought to deploy the military to Chicago during an immigration crackdown last year.
The Needle
is live
. It shows Democrats with a significant advantage in the House and an advantage in the Senate, based on returns from dozens of counties and precincts across the country.
Live Forecast: Senate and House ›

updates.headline: Update from Leanne Abraham and Arfa Momin

content.text: In Dearborn, Mich., the city clerk, George Darany, said a precinct in the city was briefly out of ballots late in the day after workers there failed to alert the clerk’s office in time that it was running low. Five people waited as officials replenished the ballots within about 10 minutes. The clerk’s office also began delivering ballot applications, which were also running low in some places, to all precincts.

Mayor Abdullah Hammoud of Dearborn sent out an alert on social media about the ballot situation amid high turnout and long lines, and recommended that everyone stay in line to vote past the 8 p.m. closing time, if need be. “Let’s keep the momentum going, Dearborn. Every vote matters!” he wrote.

Earlier this evening, I was at a polling site in South Portland, Maine, where the Democratic nominee for Senate, Troy Jackson, stopped by to shake voters’ hands and deliver his closing argument to reporters. Jackson described himself as a “change agent” and argued that voters had had enough of the Republican incumbent, Senator Susan Collins.
We have our first competitive House race where most of the vote is counted:
Florida’s 13th Congressional District

, where Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican, leads by less than 0.2 points in a Trump +13 district with 95 percent of the vote counted. This race was rated “lean Republican” by the Cook Political Report, and it’s the first clear sign that Democrats are highly competitive in usually safely Republican districts.
Florida 13th Congressional District Election Results ›

Margins are expected to tighten in the Senate race in Georgia. Many of the metro Atlanta counties have reported results from early and mail-in ballots, which are leaning Democratic. But there are a lot of votes to come that are expected to benefit Mike Collins, the Republican nominee, including results from ballots cast on Election Day as well as from rural areas in the rest of the state.

The Democratic nominees for governor and Senate in Florida are very different types of Democrats, yet they are running close together so far. David Jolly, the nominee for governor, is a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat. Angie Nixon, the nominee for Senate, is a democratic socialist. Both are garnering roughly the same share of the vote so far.

The Senate race in Ohio, where polls just closed, was America’s most expensive general election this fall, clearing the $500 million mark in advertising spending. Republicans spent about 60 percent of the money used on the airwaves in that state, all part of an attempt to help the relatively little-known Republican incumbent, Senator Jon Husted. Some of that differential is attributable to the crypto industry. Husted was helped in the end by a crypto super PAC called Fairshake,
which spent over $46 million to try to oust Husted’s Democratic opponent, Sherrod Brown

Since 2008, just two Democrats have won a partisan statewide contest in Ohio: Sherrod Brown, who is back on the ballot this year after narrowly losing his bid for a fourth Senate term in 2024, and Barack Obama, who won the state twice before President Trump carried it by wide margins in each of his presidential campaigns.
Brown’s fortunes will partly hinge on a corridor of working-class counties in northern Ohio that backed both Obama and Trump, like
Mahoning
and
Portage

. Brown will also seek to cut into Senator Jon Husted’s margins in the Appalachian corner of the state that borders West Virginia. That was where he outperformed Kamala Harris the most in 2024. Keep an eye on
Delaware County
, too: Home to some of suburban Columbus, it’s a rare area in Ohio where Democrats have gained ground in recent years.

One worry that Republicans have had in Florida is that close statewide races — even if they are eventually won by Republicans — would mean stronger Democratic turnout in House races, possibly leading to surprises and upsets in a state where Republicans currently hold 20 out of 28 congressional seats.

The first vote drops in Florida were remarkably strong for Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate, who was winning early votes in the majority-Hispanic counties of Miami-Dade and Osceola by 10 and 24 percentage points. Both of those counties had flipped to Republicans in 2024.

A rightward shift is likely to happen once Election Day votes start reporting in these counties, particularly because the partisan gap between Florida’s Election Day votes and early votes is smaller than it was two years ago.
Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, a Republican congresswoman with celebrity status in MAGA circles,
appears to be locked in a tough fight
with Leela Gray, a retired Army brigadier general and a Democrat, in her St. Petersburg-based district.

Whatever happens tonight, the results will look very Democratic for the next half hour or longer — including in states where Democrats are considered underdogs, like Florida or South Carolina. That’s because most of these states report their early votes first, and the early vote was heavily Democratic this year. Republicans hope to counter with votes cast on Election Day, which will be reported later on.

President Trump appears to be watching Fox News, and he isn’t happy with what he’s seeing. The president has denounced the cable channel in three Truth Social posts within a span of 95 minutes, accusing the network of “spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” He added, at 7 p.m., that Fox News’s ratings were “way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!”

bylines.displayName: Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Brian Oh, Stephanie Swart and Edward Vega

content.text: In Georgia, where polls just closed, the first batches of votes typically consist of ballots cast by those who voted absentee or early in-person. Margins may significantly shift as ballots from Election Day voters are posted.

One contest to watch in Florida, where most polling places have begun to close, is the governor’s race. Florida has leaned Republican the last few elections. But life in the state has gotten very expensive, and that is one statewide race — between David Jolly, the Democrat, and Byron Donalds, the Republican — that both parties found to be much more competitive than they expected going into the midterms.

updates.headline: Update from Leanne Abraham and Arfa Momin

content.text: The incumbent Republican in Indiana’s Third Congressional District, Representative Marlin Stutzman, who is trailing with just 39 percent of votes reported, is a lawmaker who rarely makes waves or national headlines, but he gained attention this year when he
introduced a plan in Congress
to phase out direct military aid to Israel in favor of a transition to a joint defense and economic investment program between the country and the U.S.
The topic was thrust back into the news this morning when President Trump said that
direct military aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year.”
Just before the polls closed, supporters of Angie Nixon, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Florida, made last-minute calls at her election-night watch party in Jacksonville to get out the vote.

At Ken Paxton’s watch party in Dallas, the campaign staff has wheeled out a cannon. It is unclear if the cannon is real or a replica. It resembles the famous cannon that became a symbol of the Battle of Gonzales in 1835, the first major military clash between settlers in what would eventually become Texas and the Mexican Army during the Texas Revolution. Paxton, a Republican, is running for the Senate against James Talarico, a Democrat seeking to win the first statewide race for his party since the 1990s.

President Trump is not expected to make a public appearance tonight, but he is sharing his real-time thoughts on Truth Social. So far, he is particularly angry about Fox News’s coverage tonight. An hour ago, Trump said he was turning off Fox because he “can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice” and would return to the channel later. Tarlov is the resident liberal on Fox News. But Trump appears to still be watching Fox because he is now criticizing its polling. “Every question is a hit job,” he wrote.

The incumbent in Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District, Representative Victoria Spartz, is an idiosyncratic figure in the House G.O.P. conference and a frequent nuisance for Republican leaders. That is in part because of her reputation for changing her mind on how she plans to vote on major legislation at the last minute, including on the Republican budget bill teeing up her party’s marquee tax and spending cuts legislation.

House Democrats are watching three key races in Florida to provide them with some early signs of how the night is going: the re-election bids of Representatives Kathy Castor, Jared Moskowitz and Darren Soto. All are Democrats who are vulnerable this year because of Republican redistricting efforts, and their races are likely to be some of the early ones that are called tonight. If they win, Democrats said they expected more good news to follow through the night.

The first votes out of Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District show an advantage for Democrats. If reporting patterns are consistent with the 2024 presidential election, that first drop is early vote. In 2024, Kamala Harris won the first drop in Hamilton County, primarily consisting of early votes, by two percentage points, before ultimately losing the county by six. Tonight, J.D. Ford, the Democrat, is winning the first drop in Hamilton County by 27 points.
Indiana Fifth Congressional District Election Results ›

Statewide race calls won’t come in Florida until 8 p.m. Eastern at the earliest. The state, where polls close at 7 p.m. local time, is mostly in the Eastern time zone except for the Panhandle, which is on Central time. The Associated Press will wait until all polls are closed across the state before declaring winners in the statewide races.

The polls at Henry Ford High School, which is in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Detroit, have been active all day with voters of all ages. Many are casting ballots for the first time, volunteers here said.

“They’re coming in like crazy, all of these cars out here on the streets, and the parking lot is full,” said Diane Roberts, 75, a poll worker who has helped run precincts in the area for the last four election cycles. “I’ve never seen anything like this.”
Democrats have been counting on high Black turnout to win the state’s competitive race for Senate. Republicans, too, have made efforts to court Black voters this year.

Turnout has been high in general, but in Florida it is running roughly on par with the 2024 presidential election, and Republicans are winning Election Day votes by a nearly two-to-one margin. The result? While Republicans led registered Democrats by just two percentage points in the advance vote — their lowest such advantage in years — they now lead by nearly nine points statewide. In 2024, they had an 11-point advantage. Of course, party registration can’t tell us much about persuasion, and any Democratic victory in Florida, where Republican numbers have surged in recent years, would come from winning over a large number of Republicans and independents.

updates.headline: Update from Christine Zhang, Laura Bult, Stephanie Swart, Sutton Raphael and Edward Vega

bylines.displayName: Christine Zhang, Laura Bult, Stephanie Swart, Sutton Raphael and Edward Vega

content.text: I’m in Anchorage, Alaska, where a handful of large signs on street corners warn voters that one House candidate, Eric Hafner, is not who he seems. Hafner is running as a Democrat but is also an inmate in federal prison whom Republicans have propped up before, and Democrats are worried that he will split votes with the independent candidate they’re backing, Bill Hill.
It’s another example of ballot stacking, the strategy that has
made headlines
after
The New York Times reported
that aides for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate, were involved in recruiting a second Dan Sullivan into the race against the incumbent Republican senator, also named Dan Sullivan.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader, just spoke briefly to reporters, projecting confidence about his party’s chances of winning the House. Still, he would not say whether he planned to call President Trump once the results were in, and he would not make projections on how big a margin Democrats might have next year.

He said he was particularly focused on watching the results in Kentucky’s Sixth District, a traditionally safe Republican district that is in play this year and could give a sense of what direction the night is taking. “Today’s vote numbers all across the country are strong,” he said. “We’ll look at Virginia, we’ll look at Pennsylvania, as two critical states, as well as North Carolina.” He said he was confident that members would be seated on Jan. 3 and that there would be a “peaceful transfer of power,” and he said that his first call after results were in would be to his mother.

Polls have closed in eastern Kentucky, the first of the night. Pre-election polls in the state showed Andy Barr, the Republican candidate running to replace Senator Mitch McConnell, leading Charles Booker, the Democratic candidate, by around nine percentage points. While that is a significant margin, President Trump won the state by more than 30 points in 2024.

For the first hour after polls start to close at 6 p.m. Eastern, Kentucky will be one of the two states reporting results. One of the earliest races to watch will be in the state’s Sixth Congressional District, where
polling

has been sparse. The only publicly released surveys have come from Zach Dembo, the Democratic nominee, or Democratic-affiliated organizations, making it likely that results are being released selectively. Still, Dembo has led in these polls since late July, including by more than five percentage points in each of the four most recent surveys.
The race remains highly uncertain, but the results may offer one of the first indications of how Democrats are performing in red districts; President Trump won the Sixth by 16 points in 2024.
Kentucky Sixth Congressional District Election Results ›

President Trump is set to start hosting an election watch party in the East Room later this evening. His Truth Social feed suggests he’s been watching Fox News, along with other coverage, none of which has indicated that a good night is coming for the bulk of his party.
Polls in South Carolina
show a surprisingly tight race. In a state that Donald Trump won by about 18 percentage points in 2024, the latest
Times/Siena poll

shows Darline Graham, the Republican senator, running neck-and-neck with Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee. Graham, who was recently appointed to the Senate after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died earlier this year, has been ahead by a narrow margin in many of the other polls.

In Juneau, Alaska, Elizabeth Thomas said Republican suggestions that the state’s top-four, ranked-choice ballots or the placement of two candidates named Dan Sullivan might confuse people were overblown. It took her just a few minutes at the Alaska State Museum to vote for Mary Peltola.

“People here know how to do it,” she said. “It’s not complicated.” Thomas, 43, works in natural resource management and said she voted for Peltola because she is part Alaska Native and agrees with her on many issues, especially environmental ones.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and minority leader, just arrived at the hotel in Washington where volunteers are phone banking, to thank them for their work. “What you all have represented throughout the last two years, which have been incredibly difficult, gives us all hope and inspiration that we are going to be able to bring about a brighter future,” he told a few dozen young volunteers who were making calls. “We’re on the brink of a dramatic change of direction in this country,” he said. “We’re on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives.”

Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, the chair of the House Democrats campaign arm, told me earlier today that she is confident Democrats will win the House majority but does not expect to have enough races called tonight to know for sure. “I’m a West Coaster so I know our numbers won’t come in until closer to 11,” DelBene said. “We might have to wait a while later tonight before all the results come in.”
Polls in Florida
show Ashley Moody, the incumbent Republican senator, with the lead over Angie Nixon in the Florida Senate race. A
Times/Siena poll
from mid-October showed Moody ahead by six percentage points. Other polls show a similar lead for the senator.
The race for governor looks quite a bit tighter than the Senate race. Still,
polls show
Byron Donalds, the Republican, with an edge over David Jolly, the Democratic nominee. The Times/Siena poll found Donalds with a four-percentage-point edge.
I’m in Bethlehem, Pa., where a hotly contested House race in Pennsylvania’s Seventh District has kept poll workers busy with a steady stream of voters all day.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, told reporters at the White House on Tuesday afternoon that he did not send federal immigration agents to polling sites today, which had been a widespread concern among civil rights and immigrant advocacy groups leading up to the election.

I’m at Ohio State University in Columbus, where volunteers are stationed around campus trying to make sure students have cast their ballots in one of this year’s most closely watched Senate races. Polls have shown Sherrod Brown, a Democrat and former senator, has some of the best odds in the country of flipping a Republican Senate seat — but in order to do so, he needs progressives like many of the students on campus to vote.

At the student union, one of the polling locations on campus, one student just told me she had waited an hour to vote for Democrats. “This year I was really big on affordability,” said Abigail Clayton, 19. She expected the line to grow even longer this evening.“I just know that people on campus don’t wake up until 2 p.m.,“ she said.
